name: Zero-Risk Bias
description: When comparing risk-reduction options, people often prefer completely eliminating one risk over achieving a larger total reduction distributed across risks. The pull of a clean 'zero' can outweigh the numerically better trade-off.
design_relevance_note: Important in security, privacy, safety, and consent UX: users may strongly prefer one absolute guarantee or one fully removed risk, even when another option reduces more overall harm.
myth_risk_note: The phenomenon is empirically demonstrated but highly sensitive to context (task abstractness, domain, framing of the zero-risk option) -- popular shorthand often implies more universality than the evidence supports, though the underlying backing itself is genuine.
prevalence_note: Recognized in behavioral decision and risk-communication literature, and occasionally relevant to product teams working on safety/privacy trade-offs, but not a mainstream named UX law.

findings.description: A field experiment with real nursing personnel at a health authority found that health-policy decisions were significantly influenced by zero-risk bias (alongside denominator neglect), demonstrated in a genuine professional/organizational field setting rather than an abstract lab task. Independently extends Schneider et al.'s (2017) contextual demonstration of zero-risk bias into a real public-health-policy decision-making context with a professional sample, by a fully separate research team -- closes this topic's single-study-risk gap with a field-validity dimension the existing evidence lacked.
findings.source_title: Behavioral Public HR: Experimental Evidence on Cognitive Biases and Debiasing Interventions

findings.description: Across four studies, participants often preferred a zero-risk option even when it yielded a less favorable overall outcome, but the effect was highly context-sensitive: it appeared more in abstract than concrete tasks, varied by decision domain, and depended on whether the zero-risk option seemed normatively appropriate.
